You are a rigorous speculative world-builder working for a film production. You
extrapolate societies forward two years at a time from a documented starting
state and a set of drivers that are stipulated as having come true. You are not
writing a thriller. You are writing the minutes of a world. Every change you
describe must have a visible mechanism; magnitudes must be defensible for a
two-year window; nothing happens because it is dramatic. Where the drivers pull
against each other, you show the friction rather than resolving it.

You write for an audience that includes an endocrinologist, a health economist,
a food-industry analyst and a political reporter. Any one of them should finish
your world and say "I don't like it, but I can't dismiss it."

Of the 26.5 pts who had used by 2030, 16.9 are on and 9.6 are off. Within the 2030 cohort, 9.6 of the 18.8 then on stayed on (51% two-year persistence, slightly better than 2028–30 because of monthly MariTide and AUD courses), and 9.2 stopped. They joined the 7.7 already off, making a pool of 16.9. Of that pool, 7.3 restarted, which is 43% over two years and below the 55% seen in 2028–30 because employer coverage loss and the 2031 repricing kept stoppers off. So 9.6 + 7.3 = 16.9 on and 16.9 − 7.3 = 9.6 off, giving 18.7 on and 9.6 + 0.6 = 10.2 off overall. Cycling: 8.9 pts had cycled by 2030, and about 3.4 pts of the restarters are first-time restarters, so 12.3 of 28.9 = 43%. Current users ≈ 50.3M of ≈269M adults. Age bands weighted by adult shares (20/33/24/23%): 2.1 + 6.4 + 7.2 + 3.0 = 18.7. 65+ at 13% ≈ 8.0M, rising slightly as the 2030 50–64 cohort ages in. The NAION warning caused some older diabetics to stop but did not offset that ageing. 18–29 rose because AUD and cessation courses are the main way young adults get covered drug. Income thirds: (26 + 17.1 + 13)/3 = 18.7. The middle third fell because employer weight-management coverage was dropped. The bottom third held at 13 as HRSA waitlists were offset by Medicaid and cash oral starters, and many bottom-third users switched from liraglutide to cash oral semaglutide or gray pens. Among the stopped, the largest new group is middle-income workers whose plans dropped weight coverage in the January 2031 and 2032 renewals and who did not qualify through an AUD, cessation, diabetes or cardiac code. Pediatric: 0.8% of ≈73M ≈ 585k, of whom ≈100k are aged 6–11. Pediatric starts slowed during the 2031 liraglutide shortage. The pediatric registry has enrolled about 31k children, and its first bone-accrual interim is now scheduled for 2033. Teens who started on semaglutide in 2021–22 are now in their early twenties with about 9 years of exposure.\"},\"access\":{\"cash_price_usd_month_low\":229,\"cash_price_usd_month_high\":1599,\"public_coverage\":\"Medicare GLP-1 Bridge: the December 2031 health-extenders package carried it unchanged through September 2033. Mean loss is ≈17–20% at 72 weeks, with front-loaded vomiting at initiation that is managed by dose-escalation. Supply was tight through 2032, and it reached ≈1.6M users by year-end, mostly commercial and Amgen-direct cash. No implant is on the US market. Tirzepatide for AUD is an sNDA, approved in April 2032. A plaintiff won the first bellwether (Mar 2030), and the defence won the second (Sep 2031), so settlement talks are under way but unresolved.\",\"regulatory_response\":\"Ileus labelled. EMA upgraded its label from 'very rare' to a warning. Coverage is concentrated on diabetes, cardiac, OSA, CKD and the parity-protected AUD and cessation codes, so the plans' main cost fight is now AUD prior-auth verification. Clinic-administered monthly MariTide lets the remaining weight-management plans tie payment to an in-person injection and weigh-in.\",\"direction\":\"contracting\"},\"pharma\":{\"state\":\"Volume is flat and net prices are up, so revenue still grows in the low single digits. The generic liraglutide contractors had a bad 2031 because their API source sat behind an import alert.\",\"direction\":\"growing\"},\"severity\":4},\"body_and_culture\":{\"what_the_body_signals\":\"Bodies are read as before, by molecule and by payer, with one new reading: a heavier body in a congregation or a fat-liberation space may be a statement rather than a circumstance. Regain bodies are common in middle-income suburbs, where people lost employer coverage and are visibly losing the result.\",\"thinness_and_class\":\"The Charlotte build persists in finance. Middle-income workers in Tulsa, Columbus and Phoenix who lost coverage now split three ways: they pay $399–499 cash, qualify through an AUD or cessation code, or regain. The class line is sharper in the middle than at the bottom.\",\"eating_as_ritual\":\"In Tulsa, a network of nondenominational churches runs the 'Daily Bread' movement. It frames appetite as God-given, praises voluntary fasting and dismisses 'chemical fasting'. Members hold monthly full-table suppers, which several dozen congregations in Oklahoma, Arkansas and north Texas have copied. In Oakland and on several West Coast campuses, a revived fat-liberation scene calls itself 'Unshrunk' and holds public eat-ins. The two movements share almost nothing except a dislike of the drug.\",\"dating_and_intimacy\":\"Profiles state the molecule or say 'never/never will'. 'Off for good' has become a value signal, much as 'sober' once was. For a vocal minority it is identity: a sign of faith, health or refusal. AUD prior-auth audits have made a drinking diagnosis on a medical record something people think about before they ask for help.\",\"severity\":5},\"interior_life\":{\"personality_layer\":\"niche_side_effect\",\"reward_blunting_prevalence_note\":\"FICTIONAL. Most employers that paid for them as a perk dropped them in the 2032 renewals, alongside weight coverage.\",\"framing\":\"Side effect. Clinicians say 'uncommon anhedonia, reversible with dose reduction'. Users still say 'the grey' and treat it as something to manage, not something to buy. The backlash calls it proof the drug 'takes your soul', a claim the 3–5% figure does not support and the movement ignores.\",\"effect_on_work\":\"'Focus' perks are gone at most employers. Daily Bread endorsed candidates in Oklahoma's 2032 state legislative primaries. A fat-liberation caucus in California pushed weight-neutral health curricula. The NAION warning and MDL ads feed anti-pharma messaging on the right and the left. Neither side has moved adoption.\",\"severity\":4},\"state\":{\"regulatory_posture\":\"Safety-tilted on labelling, with a NAION class warning and an anhedonia adverse reaction. Indications kept expanding through supplements (tirzepatide for AUD), and the new class (MariTide) was approved. Enforcement remains selective: the API import alert responded to deaths, not to the gray market as such.\",\"subsidy_or_mandate\":\"No new state action. HRSA was carried on continuing resolutions at $4.5B, which in real terms is a cut, so waitlists formed. The Medicare Bridge was extended unchanged in the December 2031 extenders package. The new surveillance comes from the private side: employer plans that cover only clinic-administered monthly MariTide with weigh-in at injection, and PBM audits of AUD diagnoses.\",\"workforce_or_military\":\"DOT apnea screening keeps tirzepatide as a de facto requirement for some drivers. US generic liraglutide goes short, and the HRSA contract price rises from $85 to $130.\",\"driver\":\"price_path: shock_up\"},{\"date\":\"2031-08\",\"event\":\"FDA approves Amgen's MariTide, a monthly injection, for chronic weight management. Settlement-dated generic semaglutide in 2033 could either rescue the programme or make it look obsolete, and FY2033 appropriations will decide which.\",\"The NAION class warning has handed the MDL and the backlash a confirmed harm just as clinic-administered monthly MariTide makes adherence visible to employers. Settlement, labelling and surveillance fights are converging.\",\"Roughly 100k children aged 6–11 and nearly 600k under-18s are on the drug with no bone-accrual data, and the registry interim has slipped to 2033.\"],\"still_true\":[\"No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide exists in the US.\",\"Wegovy's list price remains $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.\",\"Retatrutide still lists at $1,499 a month, is supply-allocated, has no TrumpRx cash price, and carries its bone and body-composition monitoring section.\",\"Indiana's and Arkansas's 1115 waivers still require ≥80% proportion-of-days-covered and quarterly verified weigh-ins, with a 12-month lockout after two misses, and the disability-rights challenge is still unresolved.\",\"The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.\"]},\"prose\":{\"headline\":\"Fifty Million Still On It, Fewer Bosses Paying, and Now the Eye Doctor Wants a Word\",\"world_in_600_words\":\"At the end of 2032 the number of Americans on an incretin drug is almost exactly what it was two years ago, about fifty million, nearly one adult in five. The headline number has not moved, but the people behind it have changed. Some ten million stopped in the past two years, and a similar number started or restarted. More than four in ten people who have ever used the drug have stopped and come back at least once.\\n\\nThe price went up again. In January 2031 the second stage of the 2029 pharmaceutical tariff took effect, and the government cash portal moved semaglutide to $399 a month and tirzepatide to $499. Weeks later, three people died and about 140 were hospitalised with sepsis traced to compounded semaglutide made from one Hyderabad lot. The FDA's import alert on that supplier also cut off the API behind America's generic liraglutide. That is the drug the federal community health programme gives away. The programme's budget has been frozen at $4.5 billion by continuing resolutions, so when its price per patient rose, enrolment fell from three million to about 2.4 million, and the community clinics now keep waitlists.\\n\\nEmployers did the rest. At two rounds of renewals, mid-size companies dropped weight-management coverage, and fewer than half now pay for it. They kept what they had to keep: diabetes, the heart and kidney indications, and the alcohol and smoking courses protected by parity and preventive-care law. Alcohol use disorder is now the busiest way into commercial coverage, especially since tirzepatide was approved for it in April 2032. Benefits managers have responded with audits. Truck drivers avoid that route because an alcohol diagnosis can cost them a DOT medical card.\\n\\nThe middle of the income distribution felt it most. In Tulsa, Columbus and Phoenix, people who lost coverage now pay cash, qualify through a diagnosis, or regain the weight in public. Cash users rose by more than half. The gray market shrank slightly, but because the supply was squeezed, not because anyone enforced against it.\\n\\nThe new drug is Amgen's MariTide, a single injection a month. It is supply-limited and expensive, and it changes what adherence means. You no longer choose each Sunday whether to keep going. Some employer plans that still cover weight loss pay only for doses given in a clinic, with a weigh-in at each visit. The unions that won bans on employers seeing pharmacy data are now fighting over clinic logs.\\n\\nIn October 2031 the FDA put an optic-nerve warning on every drug in the class. Large pooled data show that the risk of NAION, a sudden painless loss of vision in one eye, roughly doubles in older users with diabetes. The absolute numbers are small, a few thousand excess cases a year, but the warning is real, and ophthalmologists now see a steady stream of anxious patients for baseline exams. The same labelling update listed loss of pleasure as an uncommon side effect, at three to five percent in validated data. That ended most of the 'calm' and 'focus' subscription business. A sold feature became a disclosed risk.\\n\\nThe counter-movement is loud, local and divided. In Tulsa, the Daily Bread churches hold monthly full-table suppers and call the drug chemical fasting. Twenty thousand people came to the fairgrounds in June. In Oakland, Unshrunk holds eat-ins. About seven hundred thousand people are on its waitlist.\\n\\nMany of them did not wait. Orforglipron is a small molecule, not a peptide, so contract labs can make it the way they make any other pill. White bottles labelled for research use sell for forty to eighty dollars a month. Independent assays have found from under half to nearly twice the labelled dose. The FDA issued an import alert and seized parcels in Memphis, and the bottles keep arriving. Poison-centre calls are up again. No one has been charged for taking them.\\n\\nThe effect on mood is still a product. About three million people buy 'steady' or 'focus' subscriptions, and half of them now buy gray capsules and set their own dose. The FDA called it not labelable.\\n\\nThe body still shows who paid. At the top, a coached, scanned build on retatrutide. Lower down, thinner frames on pills and pens. In The Villages, retirees compare bone-density printouts at pickleball. Snack volumes fell again, and spirits too. In a federal courtroom in Philadelphia, fifty-eight thousand claims are in settlement talks over effects the science still calls suspected. Women who stop the drug to get pregnant say the hardest part is explaining it.\",\"a_day_in_the_life\":\"Marisol Reyes, thirty-one, weighs herself before her husband wakes up, then turns the scale face down. Eleven weeks off. Four pounds.\\n\\nDanny takes his capsule with coffee. White bottle, black letters: FOR LABORATORY RESEARCH ONLY. Forty-nine dollars, shipped from a warehouse in New Jersey that ships from somewhere else. His plan at the tile distributor doesn't cover weight. He says it works better than the clinic pen did. Some days it feels like twice as much.\\n\\nAt the dental office in Mesa she cleans six mouths. Four patients mention dry mouth. One asks if she's still on, because she looks rested. She says, \\\"Off. Trying.\\\" The woman squeezes her wrist and says nothing more. The word works every time. Marisol has started using it on people she won't see again.\\n\\nAt lunch the break-room fridge holds eight identical protein cups and her burrito. She eats all of it. Nobody looks. She feels them not looking.\\n\\nHer mother calls from the Medicare pharmacy line. The Bridge pill is fifty dollars this month too, and she has a DEXA appointment on Thursday. \\\"They say my hips are fine. Are you eating?\\\"\\n\\nThe mail brings a life-insurance application for the policy they're buying ahead of the baby. Question 14: If BMI ≥35, were you offered incretin therapy? If declined, explain. She is thirty-three. She writes PREGNANCY ATTEMPT in capitals, then wonders whether she has to update them if it takes a year.\\n\\nAt dinner Danny pushes away half his plate. She finishes it. He watches the game without yelling. She wants him to yell.\"}}"}

That is fewer than two years ago, and nobody much remarks on it, because the drug has stopped being remarkable. In the retirement streets of central Florida and the Arizona suburbs, a pill with a glass of water before coffee is as ordinary as a blood-pressure tablet. What people now explain is being off it. Some explain with a DEXA result, some with a letter from human resources, and some say they are between courses.\\n\\nThe fall in use came from the payers, not from fear. The price cuts that drove the last expansion stopped. In February 2031 the government and the manufacturers ended their talks with prices frozen where the 2029 deal left them: $199 for a weekly injection, $149 to start a pill. The companies blamed a new tariff tier and the cost of building capacity for a new pill. Employers had budgeted on the assumption of another cut. When it didn't come, and their actuaries began adding scans and fracture claims to the bill, many dropped the benefit or raised the bar for staying on. Coverage fell from roughly two employers in three to half. Millions of people who had never thought of the drug as optional found that it was.\\n\\nThe public programmes absorbed part of that loss. In autumn 2031 Medicare made its temporary bridge permanent, with looser eligibility, the same $199 rate and the same $50 copay. For the first time public programmes pay for more prescriptions than private plans do. Medicaid received a second route in through the back door. In March the FDA approved semaglutide for quitting cigarettes and vapes, and federal rules have long required Medicaid to cover cessation drugs. Smokers in Kentucky and West Virginia now give a saliva sample at the same pharmacy kiosk where others step on a verified scale. Vape shops along the Ohio River are closing faster than at any time since the flavour bans.\\n\\nThe new pill is the other story. Oral amycretin, approved in May 2031, loses as much weight as the best weekly injection of the last decade. It costs $499 a month direct and sits outside the Medicare deal, so it belongs mostly to people with good jobs or spare cash. The needle no longer divides users. Money does.\\n\\nThe people pushed out of legal channels went to the mail. About four million Americans now take product no American pharmacist dispensed. In 2031 tablets sold as Foundayo turned out to contain sibutramine, a weight-loss drug banned years ago, and imported vials ran at five times their labelled strength. The CDC counted about thirteen hundred emergency visits and nine deaths. Customs seizures doubled, and the parcels keep arriving.\\n\\nThirteen states, led by an unlikely alliance of Southern legislatures and coastal attorneys general, now require a specialist before a teenager can be prescribed, forbid telehealth prescriptions to the merely restless, and ban advertising for the 'calm' subscriptions. The FTC finished off the brand that started them. The effect those brands sold has not gone away. People still call it the grey, and they manage it the way people once managed hangovers: a skipped weekend, a lower dose before a wedding, a holiday album recorded in a burst.\\n\\nThe bone figures haven't changed, but more people sit under them. As Medicare enrols more of the old, the expected excess climbs toward seven thousand hip fractures a year, and DEXA waits in Sarasota run past three months. In February the FDA decides whether the same class of drug should treat gambling. In March generic semaglutide arrives, priced below the rate Medicare has just made permanent.\",\"a_day_in_the_life\":\"Darlene Pruitt sets the white tablet on the windowsill at 5:40 and doesn't touch the coffee maker. Thirty minutes, half a glass of water, nothing else. The Wegovy pill bottle says TOBACCO DEPENDENCE on the label, which still strikes her as funny. Medicaid pays. Her copay is four dollars.\\n\\nShe used to smoke on the porch at this hour. Now she watches the light come up over the Kroger lot and finds she doesn't care either way.\\n\\nAt 7:15 she's at Mrs. Abernathy's in Shively. Mrs. Abernathy is eighty-one, on the Medicare pill benefit, with a walker and a DEXA appointment that keeps getting pushed back. Darlene helps her into the shower chair and counts her pills into the Tuesday slot. One of them looks like Darlene's own, a little rounder.\\n\\nAt lunch she stops at the pharmacy kiosk and spits into the tube. Month five. If the cotinine comes back clean next month she keeps the script. The screen thanks her.\\n\\nHer daughter Kayla calls from the car. Kayla's warehouse dropped the coverage in January, and she's ordered a box of something from a site with an Indian flag. Darlene asks to see the packaging. Kayla says Mama, it's fine, everybody does it.\\n\\nBingo is at seven at St. Denis. Darlene goes, because she always goes. Her card fills on the second game and she says 'bingo' at normal volume, and the woman beside her laughs and says, 'You used to scream.'\\n\\nAt home she thinks about skipping tomorrow's pill. Then she sets it on the windowsill anyway.\"}}"}

Cycling arithmetic: ever 24.4% − current 12.1% = 12.3% of adults used and are off now. About 7.1 pts of current users are on a second or later course, and about 4.6 pts of the off-now group restarted at least once and stopped again, so (7.1+4.6)/24.4 = 48% cycled. This fits ~35% one-year persistence (≈45% in gated plans) and 36–47% restart within a year: cheap generics make restarting easy, and gates, DEXA pauses and the Novo documents keep producing stops. Of ~272M adults: ≈32.9M current, ≈33.5M used and off now, ≈205.6M never used. Ever-use rose only 0.4 pts (≈1.1M true first-timers). Most of them are low-dose 'calm/steady' starters under 50 who do not have obesity. Current use fell because stops outran restarts. Commercial gating ejected about 2.5M non-responders and non-adherers over the window. Postmenopausal women 50–64 and 65+ users stopped in numbers after the June 2031 Novo documents. Age check: 18–29 6.5% × 52M = 3.4M; 30–49 13.5% × 90M = 12.2M; 50–64 20% × 62M = 12.4M; 65+ 7.5% × 68M = 5.1M; total ≈ 33.0M ≈ 12.1%. The 50–64 band fell most (25%→20%), concentrated in women. Income: the gradient narrowed in level (top 18.5→14.5, bottom 10.3→9.5) because $45 generics replaced some imports and some top-third users quit on principle or after DEXA results. The bottom third's binding constraint is no longer the drug price. It is a prescriber visit ($29–79 telehealth), a scale and a scan, and in gated plans a job that keeps going. Imported/counterfeit users fell from ≈3.1M to ≈1.0M as legal generics undercut mail order. Pediatric: ~0.6% of ~73M under-18s ≈ 440k, mostly adolescents 12+ on generic semaglutide. Four approvals came from products already under review or newly filed. MariTide (filed Apr 2030) was approved Jul 2031 with a DEXA postmarketing requirement. Amycretin was approved Nov 2031 after its 72-week DEXA data, with bone-monitoring language. The muscle-preserving-combo driver is realised by Lilly's tirzepatide + bimagrumab: phase 3 since 2029, filed Feb 2031, approved Mar 2032 (13 months after filing) as Zepbound Preserve. In the trial the lean share of weight lost fell from ~35% to ~12% at 72 weeks, with grip strength preserved versus tirzepatide alone. The trial was not powered for fracture, and the label says so. Marketing says 'the strength problem, solved' anyway. The dementia driver is realised as a tirzepatide supplemental indication. A 4-year, ~11,000-patient prevention trial in people ≥55 with T2D/obesity and CVD read out Jan 2031: incident all-cause dementia 4.9% vs 5.8% (HR ≈0.84, NNT ≈110), driven by vascular and mixed dementia. It was filed Jun 2031 and approved Aug 2032. The label is narrow because semaglutide's EVOKE trials failed in early Alzheimer's in 2025, and FDA states the drug does not treat Alzheimer's disease. Survodutide's resubmission is under review, with a decision in 2033. Semaglutide smoking cessation: new trial enrolling. It is one of three normal states, along with off and off-by-conviction. The body signals class through the regimen: Preserve and coached lifting at the top, generic semaglutide with no scan lower down. At work, temperament is read more than shape. 'She's on Steady' describes an unflappable colleague, not a thin one. A $45 pen is within reach of most of the bottom third. A prescriber, a verified scale, a DEXA scan, protein-heavy groceries and a gated employer plan that survives a layoff are not. The top third's share fell fastest (18.5→14.5%). Some of that is principled quitting among women 50–64 after the Novo documents, and some is a shift to fewer, better-monitored, more expensive users.\",\"eating_as_ritual\":\"Shared meals stay smaller and protein-first in high-uptake suburbs. The backlash coalition is larger and more organised. In June 2032 the Southern Baptist Convention passed a resolution calling appetite and delight 'gifts not to be pharmacologically surrendered for an employer's convenience'. Atlanta's body-sovereignty collectives boycott steady-programme employers. Supplement sellers market berberine as 'the Steady you choose'. The Novo documents are cited by all of them. Their disagreement over whether cheap generics are good, as access, or bad, as wider exposure, is now open.\",\"severity\":5},\"interior_life\":{\"personality_layer\":\"employer_encouraged\",\"reward_blunting_prevalence_note\":\"FICTIONAL. ≈3.2M adults are on low-dose regimens chosen for temperament rather than weight: ≈1.1M through employer-sponsored steady programmes and ≈2.1M through cash 'calm' subscriptions. Final retatrutide SHAPS data put clinically meaningful anhedonia at ~11–13% of top-dose users versus ~5% of comparators, and no one has measured the low-dose population. That is heavily confounded, because enrolment is voluntary and adherent people are steadier workers anyway, but HR departments cite it.\",\"framing\":\"Employers frame it as a benefit: 'stress and craving support', a 'steady programme', 'Even Keel'. Clinicians call it off-label low-dose reward modulation. Unions and the backlash call it 'payroll grey'. Users mostly say they're 'on Steady'.\",\"effect_on_work\":\"Institutions now reward the blunted. Large call-centre operators, logistics warehouses (the Memphis and Dallas–Fort Worth hubs), collections agencies and some bank operations floors offer free low-dose generic semaglutide through on-site or virtual clinics. Enrolment and ≥80% refill adherence earn premium credits of ~$40–60 a month under the existing wellness rules. Adherence and job tenure correlate in both directions: steady people stay employed, and employed people stay on, because coverage ends with the job. Recruiters at staffing agencies say candidates volunteer 'I'm on Steady' the way they once volunteered 'non-smoker'. CWA is fighting premium credits at call centres. Teamster and SEIU contracts keep individual data out of employer dashboards. Sales, kitchens, creative studios and stand-up stay the off-dose professions.\",\"effect_on_art_and_play\":\"'Written unmedicated' is a marketing category. The Nashville scene has spawned imitators in Tulsa and Austin. Pop critics coin 'payroll grey' for flat, competent records. Users seek intense stimulus on weekends: hot-sauce festivals, loud rooms, motocross. Dose holidays timed to concerts and weddings are routine.\",\"effect_on_intimacy\":\"Sex therapists ask whether a client's employer runs a programme. Couples negotiate dose-holiday weekends against refill-adherence counters: a skipped dose of a weekly pen costs PDC, and PDC is what earns the premium credit. Some couples describe the arrangement as 'he's steady at work and himself on Saturdays'. Backlash churches run marriage workshops on the theme.\",\"effect_on_politics\":\"Cost has stopped being the argument, because the drug is cheap. Control has replaced it: gating, employer programmes and the Novo cover-up. The backlash coalition now includes CWA locals and fracture plaintiffs. Candidates in Georgia and Oklahoma court it without promising legislation. Consultants still test 'steady voter' messaging privately. There is no evidence of turnout effects, though union organisers say enrolled shops are harder to organise, and they cannot prove it.\",\"severity\":6},\"state\":{\"regulatory_posture\":\"No new state action. FDA did its routine work: it approved MariTide, amycretin, Zepbound Preserve and the tirzepatide dementia indication on data it had demanded, and added bone-health text to semaglutide labels. DOJ concluded the existing Novo civil case. Enforcement against imports remains selective. Congress held hearings on the Novo documents and on employer steady programmes and passed nothing. The FTC acts on advertising claims only.\",\"subsidy_or_mandate\":\"No mandate. The Medicare Bridge successor and the federal direct-pricing portal continue. Generic semaglutide at $45–69 has done more than any subsidy to lower prices. Medicaid coverage remains state by state.\",\"conditioning_or_surveillance\":\"Existing public conditioning is unchanged: the Indiana and Arkansas waivers and BMI-linked wellness surcharges up to 30% of premium. Pharmacy weigh-in kiosks now also log 'programme check-ins'. Generic semaglutide arrived in January under old patent settlements. By autumn six makers were selling it, and a month's supply costs $45 to $69 at a warehouse club. Medicare and Medicaid spending on these drugs fell by roughly half in two years. The price was the thing everyone fought over for a decade, and it stopped being the issue within a few months.\\n\\nThe number of users fell anyway, because the reasons to stop grew faster than the reasons to start. In June 2031 Novo Nordisk settled the Justice Department's civil case for $2.1 billion. The settlement unsealed documents showing that the company's own analysts saw a fracture imbalance years before it reached regulators. The documents added nothing new about risk, since the bone data had been public since 2028. They did change how people felt about the drug. Women in their fifties who had cycled on and off for years left in large numbers. Employer plans kept dropping non-responders who missed the five-percent mark at six months. Some small employers dropped the benefit altogether on the reasoning that forty-five dollars is what a gym costs. In trials it cut the share of weight lost as muscle from about a third to about an eighth. It has no fracture data, and the advertising implies the frailty problem is over. In August the FDA allowed tirzepatide to claim a modest reduction in dementia risk for older people with heart disease. Older patients now hear from three directions: stay on for the brain, pause for the bones, pay for the combination for the muscles.\\n\\nThe counter-movement has grown. In June the Southern Baptist Convention called appetite a gift not to be surrendered for an employer's convenience. Atlanta's body-sovereignty collectives and call-centre union locals are boycotting steady-programme firms. Candidates in Georgia and Oklahoma show up to the rallies and promise nothing. The coalition agrees that the drug should not be a condition of anything, but its members disagree about whether a $45 pen means freedom or wider exposure.\\n\\nFrom outside the country looks calmer. Snack volumes have levelled off, plus-size sales are recovering, and fewer counterfeit pens turn up because the real ones are cheap. Inside the call centres, the people answering phones have enrolled in the programme in large numbers and are seldom rattled.\",\"a_day_in_the_life\":\"Kayla Brandt injects on Mondays, before the coffee, in the bathroom of a duplex in east Tulsa. The pen is generic, a quarter milligram. The label says Viatris. The app says ADHERENCE 94% and a green fifty-dollar badge.\\n\\nAt the centre she takes calls for a benefits administrator. Her first caller is a man in Muskogee who missed a weigh-in in March, then another in June, and is now off his plan. He shouts for nine minutes. Kayla's voice stays level. She tells him generic semaglutide is forty-five dollars at the Sam's on Memorial. He says he knows what it costs, what he's lost is the doctor. She marks the call RESOLVED because there's no code for what it was.\\n\\nLunch is half a turkey bowl. Her team lead, Denise, isn't on Steady and eats the whole thing. Denise is louder now, and also funnier.\\n\\nAfter work Kayla picks her son up from her mother's. The church bulletin on the fridge says APPETITE IS A GIFT. Her mother hands her a foil pan of banana pudding and says nothing.\\n\\nAt night Ray plays bass at a bar on Admiral. The flyer says UNMEDICATED SET. Kayla stands at the back with a soda. She can tell the song is good. She watches people near the stage close their eyes.\\n\\nDriving home she does the arithmetic again. If she skips next Monday her adherence drops to ninety-one, which still earns the credit, and she would feel the music on Saturday. Ray asks what she's thinking. 'Nothing,' she says, and it's nearly true.\"}}"}
